To intern someone means to officially confine or detain a person against their will — essentially to lock them up or restrict them to a specific place — without putting them through a normal criminal trial. A government or military authority is almost always the one doing this.

The person being interned has not necessarily been proven guilty of a crime through a court of law. Instead, the authority decides, often out of fear, suspicion, or as a wartime security measure, that this person needs to be contained.

Imagine a regular prison sentence. Normally, someone commits a crime → they are arrested → they go to court → a judge or jury finds them guilty → they go to prison. There is a full legal process.

Interning someone skips or bypasses much of that process. The authority simply says: "We consider you a threat or a risk, and so we are confining you." The person is held — often in a special facility called an internment camp — not as punishment for a proven crime, but as a precautionary or political measure.

Historically, governments have interned people in situations like these:

During wartime: If Country A is at war with Country B, the citizens of Country B who happen to be living inside Country A may be interned. They are called enemy aliens. Even if they are perfectly ordinary, harmless people, the government may intern them simply because of their nationality, out of fear they could be spies or sympathizers.

For political or security reasons: A government may intern people it considers politically dangerous — dissidents, suspected rebels, or members of groups it views as threats — without waiting for a formal trial.

During civil conflict or unrest: In times of serious internal strife, authorities sometimes intern large groups of people to suppress resistance or maintain control.

During World War II, the United States government interned tens of thousands of Japanese Americans — people of Japanese descent who were living in the U.S. — by forcing them into enclosed camps. These individuals had not been tried or convicted of any crime. They were interned purely because of their ethnicity and the government's wartime fear and suspicion. This is one of the most well-known and widely studied examples of internment in history.
The Key Things That Define "To Intern"

To make sure the meaning is crystal clear, here are the defining features of this verb:

1. It is done by an authority. Only a government, military, or similarly powerful body interns people. An ordinary person or private group cannot "intern" someone — that would simply be kidnapping.

2. No full legal trial is required. This is the sharpest difference from regular imprisonment. You can be interned based on suspicion, nationality, political beliefs, or perceived risk — not necessarily because a court found you guilty of a specific crime.

3. It is usually tied to exceptional circumstances. Internment is not everyday law enforcement. It almost always happens during wars, political crises, states of emergency, or conflicts. It is considered an extreme measure.

4. It is not permanent by design. Internment is typically meant to last for the duration of a crisis (e.g., the war), after which the interned people may be released. This is different from a life sentence, for example.

5. It can affect groups, not just individuals. Unlike a normal criminal prosecution, which targets one specific person for one specific act, internment is often applied to entire categories of people — all citizens of a certain country, all members of a certain group, etc.
The Feeling and Weight of the Word

"To intern" is a serious, heavy word. It almost always carries a negative connotation, because it represents the use of power to restrict human freedom without the full protection of law. When you read that a government "interned" a group of people, it is a signal that something harsh, controversial, or even unjust may have occurred. Historians, human rights advocates, and legal scholars often examine cases of internment critically.

Once you know the verb, these connected words will make immediate sense to you:

  • Internment (noun) — The act or condition of being interned. "The internment of civilians during the war was widely condemned." Think of it as the name for the whole situation or policy.
  • Internee (noun) — The person who has been interned. "The internees were held in camps for three years." Just as an employee is someone who is employed, an internee is someone who is interned.
  • Internment camp (noun phrase) — The physical place where interned people are held. It is a guarded facility, separate from ordinary prisons, set up specifically to hold internees.
How to Spot It in a Sentence

Here are a few example sentences showing the verb in action:

  • "The government decided to intern all foreign nationals living in the border region."
  • "Thousands of civilians were interned during the conflict and held without charge."
  • "The military had the authority to intern anyone suspected of collaboration with the enemy."

In each case, notice that a powerful body is doing the interning, the people being interned have not gone through a normal trial, and the context involves some kind of crisis or conflict.

You may already know the word intern as a noun — a student or recent graduate working at a company to gain experience. That is a completely separate word that just happens to be spelled and pronounced the same. The verb "to intern" (meaning to confine) and the noun "intern" (meaning a trainee worker) are unrelated in meaning. Always look at the context of the sentence to know which one is being used. If someone says "She was interned for two years," they almost certainly mean she was confined — not that she had a job placement.
